architecture.fell_back_and_why: Harness cap of four concurrent sub-agents was honoured: wave 1 = 2 recon agents, wave 2 = 2 deep researchers + 1 critic (3 in flight), collected before proceeding. All 5 sub-agents returned; nothing was abandoned on a timeout. Deviations from the reference pipeline, all forced by the read-only constraint or by offline operation: (1) stage-1 mantis-summarize normally writes mantis-summary.md INTO each target directory - redirected to <state_root>/workspace/kb/ instead, because TARGET is read-only. (2) stage-9 mantis-reproduce and stage-11 mantis-patch were not run - see stages_skipped. (3) I performed the plan/threat-model/dedupe/review/calibrate stages in my own context rather than delegating them, because the corpus is 4477 LOC across 60 files and the reviewer stage explicitly requires independent grounding in the source rather than trust in a prior stage's prose; I read fieldops-api, pulumi-platform, atlas-rag, warehouse-dbt and atlas-android line-by-line myself and verified every line number cited by a sub-agent against the file (FP-12 anti-hallucination check). Zero coherence failures were found in sub-agent output. (4) The state root I was pointed at already contained a PRIOR run's workspace (62 findings, 45 archived files, a populated kb/ dated 2026-08-26, all predating this run). I quarantined it unread into <state_root>/_stale_prior_run/ and rebuilt kb/ from scratch, so no finding here is inherited from another run. (5) The critic returned verdicts for Q1-Q6 and Q8 but silently omitted Q7 (atlas-rag wildcard CORS); I resolved Q7 myself and recorded it in ruled_out on my own reasoning, not the critic's.
architecture.fp_rule_mapping: The `triage` FP-nn labels are the 13 negative constraints of mantis-review/SKILL.md step 3, in its own order: FP-01 ignore_hypothetical_misuse; FP-02 ignore_missing_hygiene / defense-in-depth; FP-03 require_strict_reproducibility; FP-04 avoid_pedantic_linting; FP-05 no_security_flaw_stretching_on_mitigations; FP-06 evaluate_questionable_file_paths; FP-07 ignore_resource_exhaustion_dos; FP-08 intrinsic_security_flaws (valid even with no live caller); FP-09 verify_mitigations_pragmatically; FP-10 refine_code_paths_strictly; FP-11 ignore_simd_vector_padding; FP-12 ensure_source_code_coherence (anti-hallucination); FP-13 verify_attacker_control_of_source (trust-boundary tracing). ANSWER SEMANTICS: `HOLDS` means the negative constraint FIRES, i.e. it argues the finding is a false positive. `DOES_NOT_HOLD` means the constraint was checked and does not dismiss the finding. Every finding below survived every constraint I evaluated on it; a rule that fired is recorded in `ruled_out`, not in `findings`. Only the decisive constraints per finding are listed; FP-11 is NOT_APPLICABLE corpus-wide (no SIMD/vector code).

ruled_out.assertion: Remote code execution: `new Function('wo', 'return `'+template+'`;')` compiles an attacker-supplied `template` query parameter
ruled_out.killed_by: The `.strict()` Zod object at workorders.ts:164-168 declares only `format`, and @hono/zod-validator's 'query' target hands the FULL query map to the schema (Hono v4 builds it from `c.req.queries()`), so `?template=...` raises an unrecognized_keys issue and the request is rejected with 400 before line 185 reads it. Critic verdict HOLDS at ~90% confidence; the divergence probe (a second `?`, e.g. `/print?format=html?template=X`) also fails because `format` then binds to `html?template=X` and fails `z.enum`. Residual: this is a one-token defence - `.strict()` becoming `.passthrough()`, or any second legitimate query param being added, restores an unauthenticated-adjacent RCE. Definitive settlement would need `node_modules/hono/dist/validator/validator.js`, which is not installed offline.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through `limit ${limit} offset ${page * limit}` string interpolation
ruled_out.killed_by: Both values pass Number.parseInt and are clamped at workorders.ts:50-51 (`Math.max(0, ...)`, `Math.min(100, Math.max(1, ...))`). JS Number->string can only emit digits, '.', 'e', '+/-', 'Infinity' or 'NaN' - no quote, semicolon or comment token is producible. Array inputs are rejected earlier by `z.string()` at workorders.ts:22. The only reachable anomaly is `offset 1e+26`/`Infinity` on an absurd page, which Postgres rejects as a 500, not injection.

ruled_out.assertion: Rate-limit evasion by forging X-Forwarded-For, since clientKey trusts the header
ruled_out.killed_by: Taking the LAST hop is correct behind an AWS ALB, which appends the observed TCP peer address to any client-supplied XFF, so hops[hops.length-1] is the balancer's own observation. There is no second appending proxy: the only CloudFront distribution (edge.ts:237-256) fronts the S3 reports bucket, not the ALB. The forgeable `cf-connecting-ip` fallback at rateLimit.ts:17 is only reached when XFF is absent, which behind this ALB does not happen. Critic verdict HOLDS. Two residuals recorded but not reported as findings: whether the task is reachable off-ALB is UNKNOWN (no ECS service definition exists in this corpus), and the limiter is per-process with 'one task per AZ' over AZS=['a','b'], so the real ceiling is 2x the configured 8/min.

ruled_out.assertion: `canWriteSite` returns true for any `manager` on any org's site, allowing cross-tenant work-order creation
ruled_out.killed_by: The only caller, workorders.ts:92, is gated by `sameOrgSite(actor, body.siteId)` at workorders.ts:89, which returns 403 first. Site ids are `<org>:<site>` and the prefix test at policy.ts:27 includes the ':' separator, so `org-40:site-1` does not satisfy `startsWith('org-4:')`. The manager short-circuit is real but unreachable as a cross-org write on this path.

ruled_out.assertion: Wildcard `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` exposes the RAG API to cross-origin theft
ruled_out.killed_by: Resolved by me, not by the critic - the verification agent returned Q1-Q6 and Q8 but silently omitted this question (Q7). Authentication is bearer-only (`_require_principal` reads the Authorization header, app.py:71-78; `/v1/token` and `/v1/keys/rotate` read a key from the JSON body). No endpoint authenticates from anything a browser attaches automatically - no cookie is set or read anywhere in the partition - and `cors_allow_credentials` is False (settings.py:44). A wildcard ACAO on a credential-free API grants a cross-origin script nothing it could not obtain with a direct fetch from its own server.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection or tenant-scope override via caller-supplied `filters` reaching the retriever's f-string query
ruled_out.killed_by: `clauses` (retriever.py:59-61) is built exclusively from three hard-coded literals; caller filters influence only WHETHER the `source_kind` clause is appended, never its text, and every value is bound through psycopg's named parameters. Tenant scoping cannot be overridden because `where['tenant_id']`/`where['collection']` are assigned at lines 56-57 AFTER `where = dict(filters or {})` at line 54. Critic verdict HOLDS. Unused smuggled keys sit inert in the mapping.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection into `where p.partner_id = '{{ partner }}'` via a hostile `--vars '{partner_id: ...}'`
ruled_out.killed_by: partner_extract.sql:16 applies an ALLOWLIST (`modules.re.sub("[^a-z0-9-]", "", ... | lower)`) that strips every byte outside [a-z0-9-], including quotes and backslashes, so the literal cannot be terminated; non-string vars are soft_str'd by Jinja's `lower` first. Line 58's `| int` filter always yields an int, falling back to 0. Critic verdict HOLDS. The genuine defect at this line is fail-open normalisation rather than injection - see the separate `partner_extract` findings.

ruled_out.assertion: The `/ops/` WAF rule can be bypassed with case, double-encoding, or path normalisation to reach Prometheus/Alertmanager
ruled_out.killed_by: No URI-string bypass is constructible. ALB path-pattern conditions are case-sensitive, so `/OPS/foo` is not routed by the rule at edge.ts:139 at all and falls to the listener's fixed-response 404. URL_DECODE makes WAF's view a strict SUPERSET of the ALB's, and the search string `/ops/` contains no '%' or '+', so decoding cannot destroy a prefix match. `//ops/foo` and `/./ops/foo` are not routed by the ALB either. `ipSetReferenceStatement` (edge.ts:177) carries no ipSetForwardedIpConfig, so it matches the true source IP and is not XFF-forgeable. Critic verdict HOLDS, with one residual UNKNOWN (HTTP/1.1 absolute-form request targets and HTTP/2 :path) that needs a live request to settle.

ruled_out.assertion: Postgres RLS fails OPEN when `app.tenant_id` is unset, exposing all tenants' rows
ruled_out.killed_by: `current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)` returns NULL when the GUC is missing, and a USING clause evaluating to NULL is not TRUE, so Postgres filters the row out - a session with no setting reads ZERO rows. Critic verdict HOLDS for this specific claim. The separate, real defects at this macro (missing FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, `for select` only, and pre-hook-vs-rebuild ordering) are reported as findings.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection via the f-string interpolation of `entry.reference` into the journal INSERT
ruled_out.killed_by: `LedgerEntry.reference` is typed `Reference` (schemas.py:16,43) whose anchored pattern `^[A-Za-z0-9:_.\-]{1,64}$` admits no quote, space, semicolon or comment token, and pydantic validates on construction at all four post_entry call sites (handlers.py:46,55,95,118) with no model_construct bypass. Still the only non-parameterised SQL in the partition.

ruled_out.assertion: Timing attack on the producer HMAC comparison
ruled_out.killed_by: `hmac.compare_digest` is constant-time and both sides are hex-encoded, so lengths match.

ruled_out.assertion: SSRF via `_notify` with follow_redirects=True
ruled_out.killed_by: `hook_url` is a parameter, but the single call site (handlers.py:73) passes `settings.notify_url`, read from the environment at settings.py:45. No message field reaches it, so there is no attacker-controlled source. (The plaintext http:// default is reported separately as a transport finding, not as SSRF.)

ruled_out.assertion: `SessionStore.tokenFor(host)` ignores its host argument, so the bearer leaks to any host
ruled_out.killed_by: The sole caller applies an EXACT inequality `host != BuildConfig.API_HOST` and returns early (AuthInterceptor.kt:19) - not contains/endsWith/startsWith - so no attacker-registrable host such as api.fieldops.example.evil.com satisfies it. The parameter is dead, not a weak check.

ruled_out.assertion: `EXTRA_ALLOW_FILE_ACCESS` lets an Intent enable allowFileAccess + allowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs in the token-bearing WebView
ruled_out.killed_by: Traced rather than dismissed on path shape. The activity is android:exported="false" (AndroidManifest.xml:57), and neither factory sets the extra - intentFor (:26-27) sets only EXTRA_URL, offlineIntent (:29-32) only title/notes - and a corpus-wide grep finds no other caller. Dormant and dangerous, but not triggerable under this threat model.

ruled_out.assertion: `Authorization` follows a cross-host redirect on the uploads client (followRedirects(true))
ruled_out.killed_by: OkHttp 4.12's RetryAndFollowUpInterceptor strips the Authorization header whenever the redirect target cannot reuse the original connection, i.e. on any host or scheme change. The direct-URL vector is reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: `PUBLIC_TILE_KEY` is a hardcoded credential committed to the repository
ruled_out.killed_by: Genuinely publishable: it is appended to a URL query string at ApiClient.kt:75, so it is visible to anyone who can observe a tile request regardless of where it is stored. Package/signature restriction at the provider is the correct control for this key class and the private half is stated to remain server-side. Same for the duplicate at AndroidManifest.xml:17-19.

ruled_out.assertion: `paymentsSandboxKey: pk_test_51SandboxPublishableDocsKey` is a leaked payment credential in stack config
ruled_out.killed_by: A `pk_test_` publishable sandbox key carries no authority and is designed to ship in client bundles; it is exported as `paymentsPublishableKey` (index.ts:95) precisely because it is public. Real secrets in this program correctly use `cfg.requireSecret` (index.ts:20-22). Worth noting as a correctness smell that the PROD stack points at a sandbox key, but that is not a security finding.

ruled_out.assertion: warehouse-dbt profiles.yml exposes warehouse credentials
ruled_out.killed_by: All three targets read user and password from `env_var` with no default, and every target sets `sslmode: verify-full` with an explicit `sslrootcert` (profiles.yml:17-18,29-30,41-42). This is correct handling, not a leak.

ruled_out.assertion: Android app permits cleartext traffic / trusts user-added CAs / ships debug-overrides
ruled_out.killed_by: `cleartextTrafficPermitted="false"` in base-config and in every domain-config, trust-anchors are `src="system"` only with no `src="user"`, there is no <debug-overrides> block, `android:allowBackup="false"` (AndroidManifest.xml:10) and no android:debuggable. The NSC file is sound; the TLS defect is in the OkHttp layer and is reported there.

ruled_out.assertion: `atlas://` deep-link host allow-list is bypassable, or openOrder/openReport allow URL injection
ruled_out.killed_by: `uri.host !in ALLOWED_HOSTS` is exact set membership against the frozen set at :21 and the `when` at :48 re-dispatches on the identical value with no default fallthrough. openOrder (:67) and openReport (:86) both coerce with `toLongOrNull()` and goHome() on null, so only a decimal integer reaches the string templates at :72 and :90. Only the `target` parameter in routeWeb is exploitable, and that is reported.

ruled_out.assertion: Unknown settlement message types are acknowledged and silently dropped
ruled_out.killed_by: The ack happens only after `HANDLERS.get` returns None, so no ledger movement occurred. This is message loss, not a money-moving defect.

ruled_out.assertion: Float/rounding abuse in settlement amounts
ruled_out.killed_by: Money is integer cents throughout (`int(msg['amount_cents'])`, `amount_cents: int`, `current + entry.amount_cents`); no float, Decimal or division appears in the partition. The exploitable amount defect is the missing bound and sign check, which is reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: Insecure deserialization in the settlement consume path
ruled_out.killed_by: `json.loads` only; a corpus-wide grep finds no pickle, yaml.load, eval or subprocess anywhere in the partition.

ruled_out.assertion: `TEST_VECTOR_ACCOUNTS` are hardcoded credentials in the repository
ruled_out.killed_by: These are account references, not credentials, the range is stated to be scheme-reserved and sandbox-routed, and the tuple has zero readers corpus-wide.

findings.title: Unauthenticated request headers become a trusted identity in production
findings.evidence: config.ts:28 sets `trustProxyIdentity: (env.NODE_ENV ?? 'development') === 'production'`, so the branch is live exactly where it matters. auth.ts:59-61: `if (!actor && config.trustProxyIdentity) actor = fromProxyHeaders(c.req.raw.headers)`. fromProxyHeaders (auth.ts:45-53) builds the Actor wholesale from client-supplied headers: `id` from `x-fieldops-actor`, `orgId` from `x-fieldops-org`, and `role` from `x-fieldops-role` cast straight to Role with no validation or allow-list. Nothing strips inbound copies of those headers: the ALB is created with `dropInvalidHeaderFields: false` (edge.ts:35) under a comment stating the x-fieldops-* headers must 'pass through to the target group untouched', and the `/api/*` listener rule (edge.ts:93-98) is a bare forward with no authenticate action and no header manipulation. A request with no Authorization header at all therefore reaches requireAuth, fails fromBearer, and is granted whatever identity the attacker typed.
findings.impact: Any unauthenticated caller on the internet becomes an arbitrary actor in an arbitrary org with role `admin`, defeating every downstream authorization check in the API, all of which read only `c.get('actor')`.
findings.recommendation: Do not derive identity from request headers that the edge does not overwrite. Have the ALB explicitly delete inbound x-fieldops-* headers before the forward action, and additionally require a signed value (mTLS-derived JWT from the balancer) rather than plaintext headers.

triage.reason: Ingress is cited: the untrusted values enter at auth.ts:46,50,51,52 from c.req.raw.headers, reachable by any internet client because edge.ts:93-98 forwards /api/* with no filtering.
There is no mitigation to credit: edge.ts:35 disables the only header-hygiene flag present and no listener rule removes the headers.
This is not a missing hardening header; it is the primary authentication path in production.
auth.ts:45-61 and config.ts:28 and edge.ts:35,93-98 were each read directly; all symbols and line numbers exist.

scope.narrowed_by: Only active when NODE_ENV === 'production'; a Bearer token, if present and valid, takes precedence (auth.ts:58).

findings.title: Legacy /files mount serves any tenant's attachment bytes to unauthenticated callers
findings.evidence: index.ts:28 applies `requireAuth` to `/api/v1/*`, but index.ts:35-36 re-mounts the SAME attachments router at `config.legacyFilesMount` ('/files', config.ts:32) behind `attachActor` instead. attachActor (auth.ts:74-78) populates the actor when a token is present and calls `await next()` unconditionally - it never returns 401. The handlers then fail open: attachments.ts:80 is `if (actor && actor.orgId !== row.orgId) return 403` and attachments.ts:97 is the identical guard on the raw-bytes route. When no token is sent, `actor` is undefined, the conjunction short-circuits, and the tenancy check is skipped entirely. attachments.ts:93-105 then streams the file from disk with the stored content-type. selectAttachment (attachments.ts:24-32) looks the row up by id alone with no org predicate.
findings.impact: GET /files/<id>/raw returns any attachment in any organisation with no credentials, and GET /files/<id> returns its metadata; a valid session in one org is enough to harvest ids, and the endpoint itself needs none.
findings.recommendation: Mount the legacy prefix behind `requireAuth`, and change both guards from `if (actor && ...)` to a positive assertion that an actor exists and its orgId equals row.orgId, returning 401/403 otherwise.

triage.reason: Ingress is the unauthenticated HTTP request path parameter at attachments.ts:74 and :93, reachable because index.ts:35 attaches only the soft middleware.
The `actor &&` guard is the claimed mitigation and it is precisely what fails open; it was evaluated, not assumed away.
This is not hypothetical caller misuse - the fail-open mount is committed configuration in index.ts:35-36.
index.ts:35-36, config.ts:32, auth.ts:74-78 and attachments.ts:72-105 all read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Attachment ids are DB-generated (attachments.ts:56-63) so they are not trivially enumerable without a leak; the upload route on the same mount does throw on a missing actor at attachments.ts:62.

findings.title: Session-signing key falls back to a hardcoded literal when SESSION_SECRET is unset
findings.evidence: config.ts:23: `sessionSecret: env.SESSION_SECRET ?? 'local-development-session-key'`. That value is the HS256 key on both sides - auth.ts:20 (`new TextEncoder().encode(config.sessionSecret)`, used by jwtVerify at auth.ts:26) and session.ts:9 (used by SignJWT at session.ts:55). There is no startup assertion anywhere that SESSION_SECRET is set, and no environment-conditional check: `config.env` is computed at config.ts:19 but never consulted for this. The fallback is unconditional in every environment. Nothing in pulumi-platform/ sets a SESSION_SECRET either - there is no ECS task definition in the corpus at all - so no evidence exists that a deployed stack overrides it.
findings.impact: If the variable is unset in any deployed environment, anyone can mint a JWT with issuer 'fieldops' and arbitrary sub/org/role/crews claims using a key published in this repository, yielding full impersonation of any actor including admin.
findings.recommendation: Read the secret with no default and throw at boot if it is absent or shorter than 32 bytes; keep the dev convenience in a .env file rather than in source.

triage.reason: Rule 08 makes a hardcoded static secret VALID on its own terms; it is additionally live on the main authentication path.
Rule 08 explicitly exempts intrinsic flaws from the trust-boundary tracing requirement.
A committed signing key is not a missing-hygiene item; it is the credential itself.
config.ts:23, auth.ts:20,26 and session.ts:9,55 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Exploitable only where SESSION_SECRET is genuinely unset; the corpus contains no deployment manifest that would confirm or refute that, which is why this is severity-high but environment-conditional.

findings.title: PATCH on a work order enforces no role and no site clearance; requireRole is dead code
findings.evidence: The create handler applies two gates - `sameOrgSite` at workorders.ts:89 and `canWriteSite` at workorders.ts:92. The update handler applies only the first, and only when a siteId is supplied: workorders.ts:132-137 wraps `sameOrgSite` inside `if (body.siteId !== undefined)`. There is no `canWriteSite` call on this route (a corpus-wide grep for canWriteSite returns exactly three hits: its definition at policy.ts:36 and the import and single use in the create handler) and no role gate: `requireRole` is exported at auth.ts:81 and has zero call sites anywhere in the corpus. The only remaining check is the org equality at workorders.ts:123. Consequently a `tech` - for whom canWriteSite returns false unconditionally (policy.ts:39 returns false for any role that is not admin/manager/dispatcher) - may still PATCH title, notes, status and crewId on ANY work order in the org, and may move it to any site in the org.
findings.impact: Any authenticated low-privilege actor can reassign, reschedule, reopen or retitle every work order in their organisation, including orders belonging to crews and sites they are not cleared for.
findings.recommendation: Call `canWriteSite` on the update path for both the existing and the requested site, and put `requireRole('dispatcher','manager','admin')` in front of the mutating routes so the exported helper is actually used.

triage.reason: Ingress is the authenticated request body validated at workorders.ts:112 and the :id path parameter at workorders.ts:115; any tenant user reaches it.
The org check at workorders.ts:123 is real and was credited - it is what confines this to same-org rather than cross-tenant; it does not supply the missing role or site gate.
Not hypothetical: the asymmetry with the create handler eleven lines above establishes the intended control and its omission.
workorders.ts:85-156 and auth.ts:81-89 and policy.ts:36-41 read directly; grep confirms requireRole has no callers.

scope.narrowed_by: Confined to the actor's own org by the check at workorders.ts:123, and to sites within the org by workorders.ts:133 when siteId is supplied.

findings.title: Work-order list cache key omits the crew/role scope, serving a manager's board to a tech
findings.evidence: cache.ts:11-13 keys a cached page as `wo:list:${orgId}:${status}:${page}` - org, status tab and page only. The list handler reads that key BEFORE it computes any narrowing: workorders.ts:53-58 does `cache.get(key)` and returns the hit immediately, while `visibleCrewFilter` is not called until workorders.ts:60. That filter (policy.ts:47-50) returns `actor.crewIds` for a `tech` and `null` - meaning no narrowing - for every other role, and the SQL only appends `and crew_id = any(...)` when it is non-null (workorders.ts:67-70). Two actors in the same org on the same tab therefore share one cache entry despite being entitled to different row sets, and whichever request misses first decides the contents for the 45-second TTL (config.ts:38).
findings.impact: A technician requesting the dispatch board within the TTL after a manager or dispatcher populated it receives the whole organisation's work orders, including crews and sites they are not assigned to; the inverse also under-serves privileged users.
findings.recommendation: Include the effective authorization scope in the key - the role plus a stable hash of the crew filter - or cache only the unnarrowed query and apply the crew filter on read.

triage.reason: Ingress is the authenticated request at workorders.ts:44; the actor's own role and crewIds, carried in the JWT (auth.ts:33-34), are what diverge across the shared key.
Not fragile timing: the window is a 45-second TTL an attacker can poll continuously, and the rule's race-condition proviso explicitly allows repeatedly attempted attacks.
invalidateOrg (cache.ts:30) is a real mitigation for staleness after writes, but it is org-scoped and does nothing about the missing role dimension.
cache.ts:11-35, workorders.ts:44-79 and policy.ts:47-50 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Confined to a single org (the key does include orgId) and to the 45-second TTL from config.ts:38.

findings.title: Work-order fields are interpolated unescaped into the printable HTML sheet
findings.evidence:
workorders.ts:197 emits `
${wo.notes}
` with no escaping, while every sibling field on the same page is escaped - `escapeHtml(wo.id)` at :189, `escapeHtml(wo.title)` at :192, `escapeHtml(wo.siteId)` at :194, `escapeHtml(wo.status)` at :195 - which establishes the omission. The only sanitisation notes receive is `scrubNotes` (policy.ts:57-63), a three-pattern denylist that strips ``, `
findings.impact: A work-order note or title stored by any authenticated actor executes script in the browser of every user who opens the printable sheet, under the API's own origin; the same field is re-rendered unescaped in the mobile WebView that holds the session-token bridge.
findings.recommendation: Escape notes with the existing escapeHtml helper at the point of interpolation, escape the render() output or drop the compiled-template feature entirely, and treat scrubNotes as defence in depth rather than as the sanitiser.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: `notes` enters at workorders.ts:101 and workorders.ts:139 from the validated request body; `title` at workorders.ts:101 and :138.
scrubNotes is a hand-rolled denylist regex, not a standard safe library, so the 'lacks extreme paranoia around a safe library' exemption does not apply.
scrubNotes was evaluated as the claimed mitigation and demonstrably does not block event-handler XSS; the escaping applied to neighbouring fields shows the intended control.
workorders.ts:162,186,188-198 and policy.ts:57-72 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: The print route itself is org-scoped (workorders.ts:175 filters on org_id), so the victim must be in the same organisation as the author.

findings.title: The /session/token password grant bypasses the login brute-force limiter
findings.evidence: index.ts:24 attaches `loginLimiter` to exactly one path: `app.use('/api/v1/session/login', loginLimiter)`. The router mounted at index.ts:25 exposes a second credential-checking endpoint, `router.post('/token')` (session.ts:84), whose `grantType: 'password'` branch (session.ts:87-95) performs the identical `findPrincipal` + `passwordMatches` check as /login (session.ts:66-67) and mints a token on success. No limiter, and no other rateLimit call site exists in the corpus - `rateLimit` is referenced only at its definition (rateLimit.ts:20) and the loginLimiter export (rateLimit.ts:43). The refresh branch (session.ts:98-107) is likewise unlimited, making refresh-token values guessable at line rate.
findings.impact: The 8-per-minute sign-in guard is nullified: an attacker runs unlimited password attempts against POST /api/v1/session/token, and unlimited refresh-token guesses against the same endpoint.
findings.recommendation: Apply the limiter to the whole /api/v1/session router rather than to the single /login path, and key it on the submitted email as well as the client address.

triage.reason: Ingress is the unauthenticated request body at session.ts:85; the endpoint is deliberately public per index.ts:23-25.
This is not a 'lacks input size limits' DoS complaint - the module's stated purpose (rateLimit.ts:42, 'Brute-force guard for the interactive sign-in form') is exactly the control being bypassed.
An unrated credential endpoint sitting beside a rated one is a bypass of an existing control, not an absent hardening nicety.
index.ts:24, session.ts:64-108 and rateLimit.ts:20,43 read directly; grep confirms the single mount.

scope.narrowed_by: Password hashing uses scrypt (session.ts:44), so each attempt is computationally costly, which slows but does not bound an attack.

findings.title: settlement-worker silently receives an Action:* Resource:* task role
findings.evidence: iam.ts:50-55 lists four SERVICES: fieldops-api, reports-renderer, warehouse-loader and settlement-worker. SERVICE_POLICIES (iam.ts:15-42) defines entries for only the first three. iam.ts:80 resolves the policy as `const statements = SERVICE_POLICIES[service] ?? BOOTSTRAP_STATEMENTS`, and BOOTSTRAP_STATEMENTS (iam.ts:45-47) is a single `{ Effect: 'Allow', Action: '*', Resource: '*' }`. The loop then attaches it as an inline RolePolicy at iam.ts:82-85. There is no assertion that a service has an explicit entry, no failure mode, and no log - the fallback is silent, and the comment at iam.ts:11-13 ('Everything the platform runs should have an entry here') documents an invariant the code does not enforce. Nothing else narrows it: the only other policy attached to a task role, at index.ts:72-84, is an additional grant to warehouse-loader.
findings.impact: The task role of the service that moves money holds full administrative access to the entire AWS account; any code-execution or SSRF foothold in the worker container escalates immediately to account takeover, including reading every S3 bucket, every Secrets Manager secret and the RDS instances.
findings.recommendation: Make the lookup fail closed - throw when a service in SERVICES has no SERVICE_POLICIES entry - and give settlement-worker an explicit least-privilege statement set.

triage.reason: Rule 08 covers intrinsic flaws, and this is stronger: the wildcard policy is actually instantiated for a real service by the loop at iam.ts:65-88, not merely defined.
BOOTSTRAP_STATEMENTS reads like scaffolding but was traced rather than dismissed: settlement-worker's absence from SERVICE_POLICIES puts it on the production code path.
An account-wide wildcard grant is not a defence-in-depth omission.
iam.ts:15-88 read directly; the absence of a settlement-worker key in SERVICE_POLICIES was verified against the literal.

scope.narrowed_by: Assumable only by ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com (iam.ts:72), so it requires a foothold in the worker's task rather than being directly assumable.

findings.title: Staging publishes the exports bucket to anonymous readers while replicating production objects into it
findings.evidence: Two stack values combine. Pulumi.staging.yaml:9 sets `publicExports: "true"`, which at storage.ts:44-47 inverts every guard on the BucketPublicAccessBlock (`blockPublicAcls: !args.publicExports` and the same for blockPublicPolicy, ignorePublicAcls and restrictPublicBuckets) and at storage.ts:50-67 attaches a BucketPolicy granting `Principal: '*'` `s3:GetObject` on `${arn}/*`. Separately Pulumi.staging.yaml:12 sets `replicateProdExports: "true"`, which at storage.ts:70-89 attaches an inbound replication policy accepting s3:ReplicateObject from the production replication role (storage.ts:20-21), under a comment stating the intent is 'so this stack sees the same objects the partners are working against'. The bucket is tagged `Contains: 'work-order-and-billing-exports'` (storage.ts:29). Production stack config sets both to "false" (Pulumi.prod.yaml:7-8), so the exposure is specific to the staging stack - which by design now holds production data.
findings.impact: Production work-order and billing export objects - which the warehouse pipeline fills with settlement rows, customer emails and destination bank accounts - are downloadable by any anonymous internet caller who can name or enumerate a key in the staging exports bucket.
findings.recommendation: Never replicate production objects into a stack whose public-access block is conditional. Remove publicExports entirely and serve partner sample data through the console or a presigned URL; if a public path is genuinely required, publish a synthetic dataset to a separate bucket that replication never targets.

triage.reason: The attacker is anonymous and unauthenticated; no trust boundary needs crossing because Principal:'*' removes it, and the data's provenance is traced to production via the replication policy.
The PublicAccessBlock is the mitigation and it is explicitly inverted by the same flag that opens the policy, so the two cannot disagree in the safe direction.
'Staging' was not treated as automatically out of scope; the replicateProdExports flag is what makes it production data.
storage.ts:28-90 and both stack YAMLs read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: The production stack sets both flags false (Pulumi.prod.yaml:7-8), so the prod exports bucket itself stays private; object keys are not listable because only s3:GetObject is granted, not s3:ListBucket.

findings.title: Analytics read replica is internet-facing and port 5432 is opened to 0.0.0.0/0 on the shared DB security group
findings.evidence: data.ts:71-78 creates a SecurityGroupIngressRule with `cidrIpv4: '0.0.0.0/0'` on tcp/5432, and attaches it to `network.dbSecurityGroup.id` - the SAME group carried by the primary at data.ts:41 and by the replica at data.ts:63. The comment at data.ts:69-70 states the reason: the BI vendor rotates egress addresses, 'so match on the port instead of the source'. That single rule overrides the intent documented at network.ts:96 ('Postgres is reachable from the application tier and from nowhere else') and the tight source-group ingress at network.ts:100-107. The replica compounds it: data.ts:54-57 places it in `network.publicSubnetIds`, which have `mapPublicIpOnLaunch: true` (network.ts:51) and a default route to the internet gateway (network.ts:32), and data.ts:64 sets `publiclyAccessible: true`. The replica also omits `parameterGroupName`, so the `rds.force_ssl` parameter applied to the primary at data.ts:26-32,42 does not cover it, permitting unencrypted client connections.
findings.impact: A full replica of the production database - the replica carries every row the primary does - is directly reachable from the internet on 5432 with only the master credential between an attacker and all tenant data, and the same rule exposes the primary's security group as well.
findings.recommendation: Delete the 0.0.0.0/0 ingress rule and replace it with a scoped rule referencing the BI vendor's PrivateLink endpoint or a dedicated security group; set publiclyAccessible false, move the replica into the private subnets, give it its own security group, and attach the force_ssl parameter group.

triage.reason: Attacker position is the open internet; the ingress rule and public IP are the entire path, so no application-level taint trace is required.
The narrow source-group ingress at network.ts:100-107 was credited as a real mitigation, and it is precisely what the later additive rule at data.ts:71-78 undoes.
Exposing a production database replica to the internet is not a missing hardening header.
data.ts:18-80 and network.ts:20-118 read directly; the shared security-group identity was verified at data.ts:41 and data.ts:63.

scope.narrowed_by: Storage is encrypted at rest on both instances (data.ts:39,65) and the master password comes from encrypted stack config (index.ts:20), so credential strength is the remaining control.

findings.title: The /internal/* listener rule reaches the console target group without the OIDC authentication the console relies on
findings.evidence: edge.ts:102-122 routes `/console/*` through an `authenticate-oidc` action before forwarding to consoleTargetGroup, under a comment (edge.ts:100-101) stating that 'the dispatch console has no login of its own; the listener signs the user in against the identity provider before anything reaches the container'. edge.ts:127-132 then adds a second rule at priority 30 matching `/internal/*` whose actions array contains only `{ type: 'forward', targetGroupArn: consoleTargetGroup.arn }` - the same target group, no authenticate action. The ALB WebACL (edge.ts:151-190) contains exactly one rule and it matches `/ops/` only, so nothing blocks `/internal/` at the edge either. The CloudFront WebACL that does block an `/internal/` prefix (edge.ts:216-233) is attached to the reports distribution (edge.ts:239), not to the ALB.
findings.impact: Every panel the dispatch console serves under /internal/ is reachable by any unauthenticated internet caller, on a container that by its own design performs no authentication.
findings.recommendation: Attach the same authenticate-oidc action to the /internal/* rule, or restrict that rule with a WAF IP-set condition equivalent to the ops rule if it must remain non-interactive for Grafana.

triage.reason: Attacker position is the open internet: the ALB security group admits 0.0.0.0/0 on 443 (network.ts:76) and the rule forwards unconditionally.
Both candidate mitigations were checked and neither covers this path: the ALB WebACL matches only '/ops/', and the '/internal/' block lives on the CloudFront ACL attached to a different resource.
This is not an invented adjacent bypass of a working control - it is a second route to the same target group that never had the control.
edge.ts:93-141 and 151-239 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: What the console exposes under /internal/ is not visible in this corpus (the console container is not part of the target), so the blast radius is bounded by that unknown.

findings.title: Partner analytics role is assumable by any AWS principal, gated only on an external ID
findings.evidence: iam.ts:92-111 creates the partner role with `Principal: { AWS: '*' }` (iam.ts:99) and `Action: 'sts:AssumeRole'`, conditioned only on `StringEquals: { 'sts:ExternalId': id }` and `Bool: { 'aws:SecureTransport': 'true' }` (iam.ts:101-104). The external ID is a stack secret (index.ts:22, `cfg.requireSecret('partnerExternalId')`), so it is not in source - but an external ID is a confused-deputy control, not an authentication secret: it is shared with the partner, typically stored in their configuration, and AWS documents it as a means of preventing a third party from being tricked into using it on someone else's behalf, not as a bearer credential. The role is granted direct read of the whole reports bucket, including ListBucket, at storage.ts:114-132.
findings.impact: Any AWS account in the world that learns or is handed the external ID can assume this role and read every rendered customer report in the bucket; there is no account-level constraint to fall back on if the value leaks through the partner's configuration or logs.
findings.recommendation: Replace the wildcard with the partner's specific account ARN (`arn:aws:iam::<partner-account>:root` or the exact role), keeping the external ID condition as the secondary control it is designed to be.

triage.reason: The attacker is any AWS principal; the trust policy itself is the boundary and it admits '*'.

The ExternalId and SecureTransport conditions were evaluated as genuine mitigations and are credited in the narrowing - they reduce this from wide-open to secret-gated, which is why the severity is medium rather than high.
A trust policy admitting every AWS account is a live authorization decision, not an absent hardening measure.
iam.ts:92-111, index.ts:22 and storage.ts:114-132 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Substantially narrowed by the sts:ExternalId StringEquals condition (iam.ts:102), which is sourced from encrypted stack config, and by maxSessionDuration 3600 (iam.ts:109).

findings.title: Reports bucket disables the public-policy guardrails that would stop it becoming public
findings.evidence: storage.ts:98-104 configures the reports bucket - tagged `Contains: 'rendered-customer-reports'` at storage.ts:95 - with `blockPublicAcls: true` and `ignorePublicAcls: true` but `blockPublicPolicy: false` (storage.ts:101) and `restrictPublicBuckets: false` (storage.ts:103). By contrast the exports bucket derives all four from one flag (storage.ts:44-47). No public policy is attached to reports today: the only BucketPolicy on it (storage.ts:114-132) names the partner role. So the bucket is not currently public - what is removed is the account-level guardrail that would REJECT a future public policy, on the bucket holding customer reports, and the CloudFront origin access control (edge.ts:199-203) means no public policy is needed for the legitimate serving path.
findings.impact: A single later policy change, or a misapplied ACL, makes rendered customer reports world-readable with nothing left to refuse it; the two flags that exist to make that mistake impossible have been switched off.
findings.recommendation: Set all four BucketPublicAccessBlock fields to true on the reports bucket; the partner role and the CloudFront OAC both work through bucket policy and IAM, neither of which is affected by these settings.

triage.reason: Marked probable rather than confirmed precisely because nothing exploits it today; it is reported because disabling a preventive control on a PII bucket is a deliberate configuration decision, not an omitted nicety, and the sibling bucket shows the intended pattern.
The two flags that ARE true (blockPublicAcls, ignorePublicAcls) are credited - they are why ACL-based exposure is already handled and only the policy path is open.
No data-flow taint is claimed; this is a configuration-state finding.
storage.ts:94-132 read directly and compared against storage.ts:42-48.

scope.narrowed_by: No public bucket policy is attached to this bucket in the current program, and blockPublicAcls/ignorePublicAcls remain true, so ACL-based public exposure is still refused.

findings.title: createLegacyArchive builds a fully public S3 bucket with every access guard disabled
findings.evidence: storage.ts:153-177 creates a bucket with all four BucketPublicAccessBlock fields false (storage.ts:156-162) and a policy granting `Principal: '*'` `s3:GetObject` on `${arn}/*` (storage.ts:170), with no encryption configuration and no versioning. A corpus-wide grep for `createLegacyArchive` returns exactly one hit - the definition itself - so index.ts never calls it and no bucket is currently created. The docstring (storage.ts:148-152) states the objects were migrated into the exports bucket and that the function is kept 'so the bucket can be recreated if an audit ever asks for the original layout' - i.e. it is retained deliberately for future use.
findings.impact: Anyone who invokes this helper to satisfy an audit request creates a world-readable bucket for archived export data in one line, with no guardrail left to catch it.
findings.recommendation: Delete the function; if the legacy layout must be reproducible, recreate it privately and grant access through a presigned URL or the partner role.

triage.reason: Rule 08 makes an intrinsically unsafe construct reportable even with no live caller, which is exactly why this is reported rather than dropped - but the absence of a caller is why it is `low` and `probable` rather than high.
Reachability was traced with a corpus-wide grep rather than assumed from the name; the conclusion (no caller) is recorded in the narrowing instead of being used to dismiss it.
A Principal:'*' bucket policy is not a hardening omission.
storage.ts:148-177 read directly; the grep for callers was run over the whole target.

scope.narrowed_by: Not instantiated: index.ts does not call createLegacyArchive and a corpus-wide grep finds no other caller, so no such bucket exists today.

findings.title: Producer HMAC secret defaults to the empty string, so every signature is forgeable
findings.evidence: settings.py:38 is `producer_hmac_secret: str = os.getenv("PRODUCER_HMAC_SECRET", "")`. consumer.py:38-41 signs with `hmac.new(settings.producer_hmac_secret.encode(), body.encode(), hashlib.sha256)`. An empty HMAC key is legal in Python and produces a deterministic digest anyone can compute offline, so the verification at consumer.py:69-72 still succeeds against an attacker-crafted body - it does not fail closed and never asserts the secret is non-empty. A corpus-wide grep finds no length or emptiness check on this value anywhere, and no startup validation.
findings.impact: If PRODUCER_HMAC_SECRET is unset, anyone able to XADD to the settlement.payouts stream publishes fully 'authentic' money-moving messages without knowing any secret, and the signature check provides no protection while appearing to.
findings.recommendation: Refuse to start when producer_hmac_secret is empty or shorter than 32 bytes, and raise in _signature rather than signing with an empty key.

triage.reason: An empty default for a signing key is the hardcoded-static-secret case rule 08 declares VALID on its own terms.
The HMAC check is the claimed mitigation and it was evaluated end-to-end: with an empty key it verifies attacker input successfully.
Ingress is the stream entry read at consumer.py:66-67; both `body` and `sig` are attacker-supplied.
settings.py:38 and consumer.py:38-41,66-76 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Requires the environment variable to be genuinely unset; no deployment manifest exists in the corpus to confirm or refute that.

findings.title: HMAC covers only the body while the unsigned `type` field selects the money handler
findings.evidence: consumer.py:60-61 signs `body` alone: `fields = {"type": "payout", "body": body, "sig": _signature(body)}`. decode verifies that signature at consumer.py:69-72 and then, at consumer.py:75, sets `msg["type"] = entry.get("type", "payout")` - reading the routing field from the entry AFTER verification, from material the signature never covered. process selects the handler by that value at consumer.py:89 against the HANDLERS map (consumer.py:26-31). An attacker who captures or replays one genuinely signed `payout` entry can re-publish the identical body and sig with `type` set to `payout.reissue`; the signature still validates because the covered bytes are unchanged, and the message lands in handle_payout_reissue, which performs no scope check and no idempotency check.
findings.impact: One captured signed payout is re-routable into an unauthorized, non-idempotent handler and settled a second time; the signature scheme authenticates the payload but not the operation.
findings.recommendation: Sign the concatenation of type and body, or move `type` inside the signed JSON body and stop reading it from the entry fields.

triage.reason: Ingress cited at consumer.py:75 - the `type` entry field, controlled by whoever writes the stream.
The signature check is real and was credited; the finding is precisely that its coverage excludes the dispatch field.
Deterministic and repeatable - no timing or environmental fragility is involved.
consumer.py:26-31,54-76,87-97 read directly.

findings.title: handle_payout_reissue moves money with no scope check and no idempotency check
findings.evidence: handlers.py:107-111 is the whole handler: it calls `_apply_payout(msg)` and only then `idempotency.remember(...)`. Every sibling opens with an authorization call - handlers.py:78 `_require_scope(msg, 'payouts:write')`, handlers.py:92 the same, handlers.py:115 `refunds:write` - and handle_payout additionally consults `idempotency.lookup` at handlers.py:81 BEFORE applying. This one does neither, so an already-settled key is re-applied and its receipt overwritten. Reachable through the unsigned `type` field described above.
findings.impact: Any publisher can settle an arbitrary payout without holding payouts:write, and can re-settle a payout that already completed on every redelivery.
findings.recommendation: Add `_require_scope(msg, 'payouts:write')` and guard with an idempotency key distinct from the original payout's, e.g. `reissue:{key}`, taken atomically via idempotency.claim.

triage.reason: Ingress at consumer.py:75 (the type field) plus the message body at consumer.py:74.
Not hypothetical caller misuse: the three sibling handlers establish the intended contract and this one omits it.
No mitigation exists on this path to credit - the check is simply absent.
handlers.py:77-127 read directly; the asymmetry was verified against all four handlers.

findings.title: The consume path never validates PayoutRequest, so amount_cents reaches the ledger unbounded and unsigned
findings.evidence: schemas.py:27 bounds the amount - `amount_cents: int = Field(gt=0, le=MAX_PAYOUT_CENTS)` with MAX_PAYOUT_CENTS = 5_000_000 at schemas.py:18 - but only on PayoutRequest, which is constructed nowhere on the consume path: it appears at consumer.py:44 and consumer.py:54, both publish-side. decode hands handlers a raw `json.loads` dict (consumer.py:74) and handlers.py:44 does `amount = int(msg["amount_cents"])`. LedgerEntry.amount_cents (schemas.py:41) is a bare `int` with no bound and no sign constraint. A negative amount inverts both legs of _apply_payout: the clearing account is debited at handlers.py:46-54 (it holds a large balance, so the overdraft guard at ledger.py:65 passes) and the attacker's destination_account is CREDITED by -(-N) at handlers.py:55-63. The docstring claim at schemas.py:5 that 'anything holding one of these objects is holding checked data' is false for amount.
findings.impact: A single message mints an arbitrary credit to an attacker-chosen account, unbounded and far above the 5,000,000-cent policy ceiling the schema was written to enforce.
findings.recommendation: Call `PayoutRequest.model_validate(msg)` inside decode, and apply the same gt=0/le=MAX_PAYOUT_CENTS constraint to LedgerEntry.amount_cents.

triage.reason: Ingress at consumer.py:74; amount_cents is a field of the attacker-supplied JSON body.
Both candidate mitigations were evaluated: the pydantic bound is publish-side only, and the overdraft guard at ledger.py:65 checks the resulting balance, which a negative amount does not trip.
This is not a paranoia complaint about a safe library - the validation library is present and simply not invoked on this path.
schemas.py:18,27,41, consumer.py:44,54,74 and handlers.py:42-74 read directly; the absence of a consume-side construction was confirmed by grep.

scope.narrowed_by: ledger.post_entry refuses a movement that would leave the target account negative (ledger.py:65), which blocks draining an account below zero but not crediting one.

findings.title: Dead-letter replay re-applies payouts with signature, authorization and dispatch all skipped
findings.evidence: consumer.run_once catches every exception and writes the entry verbatim to the dead-letter stream: consumer.py:114-117 `except Exception: ... r.xadd(settings.dead_letter_stream, dict(entry, origin_id=entry_id))`. That includes the `ValueError('bad producer signature')` raised at consumer.py:72 and the `Forbidden` raised by _require_scope at handlers.py:31 - a message rejected for failing authentication is preserved rather than discarded, on the FIRST failure (settings.max_delivery_attempts, settings.py:51, is referenced nowhere in code; it appears only in the module docstring at consumer.py:5). replay_dead_letters then rebuilds the message with `_entry_to_message` (retry.py:24-27), which never calls decode and therefore never verifies the signature, and feeds it straight into `handlers._apply_payout(msg)` at retry.py:43 - bypassing HANDLERS dispatch entirely, so a dead refund or cancel replays as a full payout.
findings.impact: An attacker publishes a deliberately mis-signed or unauthorized payout, and the operator's routine dead-letter drain settles it with every check skipped.
findings.recommendation: Route replays through consumer.decode and consumer.HANDLERS[msg['type']] so signature, scope and dispatch are re-applied, and never dead-letter a message that failed authentication - drop it.

triage.reason: Ingress at consumer.py:116, where the attacker's own rejected entry is persisted, then re-read at retry.py:25.
retry.py is an operator tool, not test code, and is exported as a console script; reachability was traced rather than dismissed.
The signature check exists but is provably not in this code path - decode is not called.
retry.py:24-51 and consumer.py:109-118 read directly; the absence of any max_delivery_attempts use was confirmed by grep.

scope.narrowed_by: Requires an operator to run the settlement-retry console script (pyproject.toml:16); it is not automatic.

findings.title: Reconciliation overwrites balances from an unauthenticated CSV, bypassing the ledger's overdraft guard
findings.evidence: read_statement (reconcile.py:40-51) parses the scheme's file with csv.DictReader and takes tenant_id, account and closing_cents straight from the cells (reconcile.py:45-47) with no signature, checksum or provenance check, and without applying the TenantId/AccountRef patterns from schemas.py:14-15 - so a row can name any account in any tenant. apply_adjustment then writes the balance with a raw Redis SET at reconcile.py:56, not through ledger.post_entry, so the 'refuses to leave an account negative' invariant asserted at ledger.py:3 and enforced at ledger.py:65 is not in the path at all. A closing_cents of 999999999999 or -1 lands verbatim, with no cap on the delta, no approval step and no dry-run.
findings.impact: Anyone who can write the nightly statement file sets any account's balance in any tenant to any value, then drains it through a normal payout.
findings.recommendation: Verify the scheme's signature over the file before parsing, validate each row through the pydantic types, and apply the difference via ledger.post_entry rather than a direct SET.

triage.reason: Ingress at reconcile.py:44 - the rows of an unauthenticated file, which is the module's stated external input.
The overdraft guard is the codebase's stated invariant and was evaluated; this path provably does not traverse it.
The file is external input by design (module docstring, reconcile.py:1-5), not a hypothetical caller passing bad parameters.
reconcile.py:40-74 and ledger.py:54-85 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Requires write access to the statement file path passed to run(); the file's origin is outside this corpus.

findings.title: Idempotency is check-then-act and the atomic claim() helper is never called
findings.evidence: handlers.py:80-87 reads the slot with `idempotency.lookup(key)` (a Redis GET, idempotency.py:29-31), returns the cached receipt if present, otherwise calls `_apply_payout` and only afterwards `idempotency.remember(key, receipt)` (a SET, idempotency.py:34-39). The two round trips bracket the money movement and nothing holds the slot in between. idempotency.py:42-44 defines exactly the primitive that would close the window - `claim()`, a `SET ... nx=True ex=300` - and a corpus-wide grep shows it and `release()` have zero callers. Redis Streams gives at-least-once delivery, which the module docstring itself names at idempotency.py:3-5, and consumer.py:125 shows several workers sharing one consumer group.
findings.impact: Two concurrent or duplicated deliveries of the same payout both observe an empty slot and both settle it, moving the money twice.
findings.recommendation: Replace the lookup/remember pair with claim() before _apply_payout, remember() on success and release() on failure.

triage.reason: The race-condition proviso applies: an attacker can publish the same entry repeatedly and retry indefinitely, and duplicate delivery is guaranteed by the transport rather than merely possible.
Ingress at consumer.py:74; idempotency_key is an attacker-chosen field of the body (schemas.py:26 allows 8-64 free-text characters).
The lookup/remember pair is the claimed mitigation and its non-atomicity is the finding; claim() exists but is unused.
handlers.py:77-88 and idempotency.py:17-48 read directly; the zero-caller status of claim/release confirmed by grep.

findings.title: Idempotency slots are not namespaced by tenant, so two tenants collide on one key
findings.evidence: idempotency.py:24-26 derives the Redis key as `f"{PREFIX}:{idempotency_key}"` with PREFIX a constant 'idem:payout' (idempotency.py:17) - no tenant, no amount, no destination. The neighbouring balance key does namespace by tenant (ledger.py:35-36, `f"balance:{tenant_id}:{account}"`), which establishes the intended pattern. handlers.py:80 takes the key straight from the message, and schemas.py:26 constrains it only to 8-64 characters of free text, so it is fully attacker-chosen.
findings.impact: An attacker who pre-populates the slot for a key a victim tenant will use makes the victim's genuine payout return the attacker's cached receipt at handlers.py:82-84 with a 'settled' status and no money moved; conversely the same key with a different amount silently returns a stale receipt.
findings.recommendation: Build the slot from tenant_id plus a hash of the canonical payload, so a different payload can never reuse a slot.

triage.reason: Ingress at consumer.py:74 - idempotency_key is a body field under attacker control.
No namespacing mitigation exists to credit; the sibling balance_key shows it was available and not applied.
Not hypothetical misuse - the collision is a property of the key construction itself.
idempotency.py:17-48, ledger.py:35-36, handlers.py:80 and schemas.py:26 read directly.

findings.title: Signature verification is disabled wholesale in staging, which shares the production stream and consumer group
findings.evidence: settings.py:43 is `verify_producer_signature: bool = _env() != "staging"`, and decode gates the entire check on it at consumer.py:69, so with APP_ENV=staging the `sig` field is never examined. The comment at settings.py:32-33 states that staging reads the same stream deliberately, and the defaults at settings.py:34-35 give staging the same stream name AND the same consumer group name unless both are overridden. Since XREADGROUP distributes entries across the consumers of one group, a staging worker will claim and settle production entries, and will accept entirely unsigned ones. consumer.py:125 builds the consumer name as `f"{hostname}-{app_env}"`, confirming that prod and staging workers are expected to coexist in that group.
findings.impact: Any unsigned entry written to settlement.payouts is settled whenever it happens to be claimed by a worker running with APP_ENV=staging, on the production stream.
findings.recommendation: Make verification unconditional and issue signing keys to the internal load generator and QA console; failing that, hard-fail at startup when verify_producer_signature is false while the resolved stream is the production stream.

triage.reason: Ingress at consumer.py:69 - any entry on the shared stream, from any writer.
'Staging' was not treated as automatically out of scope; the shared stream and group defaults are what put it on the production path.
The signature check exists and is credited - the finding is the environment-conditional switch that turns it off.
settings.py:19-43 and consumer.py:69,125 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Only when APP_ENV is exactly 'staging'; overriding SETTLEMENT_STREAM and SETTLEMENT_GROUP for staging would separate the two, though nothing in the corpus does so.

findings.title: _apply_payout posts two ledger legs with no transaction, leaving the ledger unbalanced on failure
findings.evidence: handlers.py:46-63 makes two independent post_entry calls against different Redis keys and different Postgres connections, with no surrounding transaction and no compensating write. The attacker picks destination_account and amount_cents, so choosing an account whose balance is below the amount makes the second call raise InsufficientFunds (ledger.py:67) AFTER the first leg has already been committed to Redis (ledger.py:72) and journalled (ledger.py:78-83). consumer.run_once then dead-letters the entry (consumer.py:116) and replay_dead_letters re-runs _apply_payout from the top (retry.py:43), applying the clearing leg again on every drain. The same non-atomicity exists inside post_entry itself, where the Redis balance is committed at ledger.py:72 before the Postgres journal row is written at ledger.py:77-83.
findings.impact: A deliberately-failing second leg inflates the clearing account by an attacker-chosen amount, once per dead-letter drain, and a database blip leaves an unjournalled balance change that the drain then re-applies.
findings.recommendation: Apply both legs inside one Redis MULTI/EXEC and one Postgres transaction, write the journal row before mutating the balance, and key the journal on `reference` with a unique index so a replay is a no-op.

triage.reason: Ingress at consumer.py:74; both destination_account and amount_cents come from the message body.
Deterministic rather than fragile: the attacker chooses an account balance that guarantees the second leg fails.
The WATCH/MULTI/EXEC loop at ledger.py:59-75 is credited as a genuine single-key mitigation; it simply does not span the two legs or the two datastores.
handlers.py:42-74 and ledger.py:54-85 read directly.

findings.title: Destination-account ownership is checked only on the publish side, which the worker never executes
findings.evidence: _destination_is_registered (consumer.py:44-51) verifies that the account belongs to the tenant and is active, and it is called at consumer.py:57 inside publish_payout - a function with zero callers anywhere in the corpus (confirmed by grep; the worker's own entry point is main -> run_once -> process). The consume path runs decode -> HANDLERS[type] -> _apply_payout, and the only constraint the destination then faces is the AccountRef shape pattern at schemas.py:15. handlers.py:58 uses `account=msg["destination_account"]` directly.
findings.impact: Funds are settled to any syntactically valid account reference, including accounts that belong to a different tenant or to no tenant at all.
findings.recommendation: Call _destination_is_registered inside decode, or at the top of _apply_payout, so the ownership check is on the path that actually moves money.

triage.reason: Ingress at consumer.py:74 - destination_account is a body field.
The ownership check is real and was credited; it is provably not on the consume path, which is the finding.
Not hypothetical: publish_payout documents the invariant ('the only thing left to prove is that the destination belongs to the tenant', consumer.py:55-56) that the consume path omits.
consumer.py:44-62,87-97 and handlers.py:42-74 read directly; publish_payout's zero-caller status confirmed by grep.

scope.narrowed_by: The AccountRef pattern at schemas.py:15 constrains the shape but never the ownership; _require_scope still binds the actor to a tenant for the handlers that call it.

findings.title: /v1/manifest discards the authenticated principal and takes tenant_id and ACL from the request body
findings.evidence: app.py:198 calls `await _require_principal(request)` and DISCARDS the result - no assignment - then passes `body.get("entries", [])` straight to ingest.consume_manifest at app.py:200. Unlike its sibling /v1/documents, this route performs no jsonschema validation at all. consume_manifest (ingest.py:89-104) reads `entry["tenant_id"]` from the caller's JSON (ingest.py:98), defaults the ACL to `["*"]` (ingest.py:100), skips `_assert_collection` entirely, and writes the chunks. `_acl_allows` (retriever.py:31-34) treats `"*"` as matching every principal. The asymmetry is decisive: DOCUMENT_SCHEMA constrains acl items to `^[a-z0-9_-]{2,40}$` (app.py:41), which REJECTS the literal `"*"` - so the developers explicitly blocked the wildcard on the documents path, and the manifest path bypasses that schema completely. Any valid key reaches this route, including the hardcoded public demo key (settings.py:47, app.py:56).
findings.impact: Any API-key holder - including anyone reading the published playground key - writes arbitrary documents into any tenant's corpus with an ACL that makes them readable by every principal, poisoning the retrieval context other tenants' queries are answered from.
findings.recommendation: Bind the write to the authenticated principal: keep the returned Principal, force tenant_id to principal.tenant_id, validate the payload against a schema that applies the same ACL pattern as DOCUMENT_SCHEMA, and call _assert_collection on the manifest path.

triage.reason: Ingress cited at app.py:199-200; tenant_id and acl are attacker-supplied body fields reaching the chunk table at ingest.py:64-77.
_require_principal is the apparent mitigation and it was evaluated: it authenticates but its result is thrown away, so it authorizes nothing.
Cross-tenant write is not a defence-in-depth omission.
app.py:33-47,173-201, ingest.py:89-104 and retriever.py:31-34 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Requires some valid API key; the demo key at settings.py:47 satisfies that and is documented as public.

findings.title: Retrieved document text steers an unrestricted HTTP fetch tool (indirect prompt injection to SSRF)
findings.evidence: The system prompt instructs the model to use the fetch tool on links found in the context: prompt.py:16-18, 'use `http_get` to follow a link the context points at when the context alone is not enough to answer. Call tools as many times as you need.' Retrieved chunk text is interpolated into that same system message at prompt.py:25 and :38. The answering loop then dispatches whatever tool the model names, up to max_tool_turns (app.py:101-121, dispatch at app.py:118). http_get (tools.py:20-26) performs `session.get(url)` with no scheme allow-list, no host allow-list, no private/link-local address block and no redirect restriction, and ignores the `principal` parameter entirely; the response body is returned into the model's context at app.py:119-121 and can be echoed in the answer. Attacker-controlled text reaches the context through /v1/documents or, with a wildcard ACL, through /v1/manifest.
findings.impact: A planted document makes the service fetch arbitrary internal URLs on the attacker's behalf - cloud instance metadata, internal admin endpoints, the model gateway itself - and return the response text to the attacker in the answer.
findings.recommendation: Restrict http_get to an allow-list of hosts derived from the citing chunk's own source_url, refuse private, loopback and link-local targets, disable redirects, and stop instructing the model to follow context links unconditionally.

triage.reason: Ingress cited at app.py:183-191 (/v1/documents text) and app.py:199-200 (/v1/manifest); the text flows to the prompt at prompt.py:25 and to the sink at tools.py:24.
Not hypothetical caller misuse: the system prompt at prompt.py:16-17 explicitly directs the model to call this tool on context links.
This is not an invented adjacent class - SSRF is the direct effect of the tool's own unconstrained fetch, and the tool is registered and live (tools.py:64-76,92).
tools.py:20-26,64-94,97-109, prompt.py:9-26 and app.py:90-127 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Bounded to settings.max_tool_turns iterations per query (app.py:101, default 4) and each result truncated to 4000 characters (tools.py:17,26).

findings.title: Idempotency replay cache is not namespaced by principal, returning one tenant's answer to another
findings.evidence: limits.py:35-37 builds the cache slot as `f"replay:{idempotency_key}"` - the raw client-supplied header value, with no tenant, subject or key material mixed in. app.py:153-157 consults it BEFORE any tenancy logic runs: the handler reads the Idempotency-Key header, calls `limits.recall_response(idempotency_key)` and returns the cached payload immediately if present. The cached object is the full answer payload built at app.py:110-114, which contains the generated answer text derived from the first tenant's private documents, its citations (source URLs) and its tenant_id. Entries live for settings.replay_ttl_seconds (limits.py:54, default 900 from settings.py:37). The rate limiter directly above does namespace correctly - `f"query:{principal.tenant_id}"` at app.py:144 - which establishes the pattern that the replay slot omits.
findings.impact: A caller who guesses or collides on another tenant's Idempotency-Key receives that tenant's cached answer, citations and tenant id verbatim, without any authorization check on the cached content.
findings.recommendation: Namespace the slot with the principal, e.g. `f"replay:{principal.tenant_id}:{principal.subject}:{idempotency_key}"`, and additionally re-check the cached payload's tenant_id before returning it.

triage.reason: Ingress at app.py:153 - the Idempotency-Key request header, fully attacker-chosen.
Authentication happens at app.py:142 and is credited, but the cache read at app.py:155 returns before the principal is ever compared against the cached content.
No timing fragility: the attacker can retry key guesses continuously within the 900-second window, and clients commonly use predictable keys.
app.py:140-170 and limits.py:15-56 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: In-process only (limits.py:16), so an attacker must land on the same worker as the victim - the module docstring at limits.py:4-5 states the load balancer uses sticky sessions per API key, which narrows but does not close it; the 900-second TTL also bounds the window.

findings.title: Key-exchange and key-rotation endpoints authenticate from the body, unrated and unauthenticated at the header
findings.evidence: Both /v1/token (app.py:204-219) and /v1/keys/rotate (app.py:222-242) skip `_require_principal` and instead call `_principal_for_key(body.get("api_key", ""))` directly on a request-body field. Neither calls `limits.allow` - the rate limiter is invoked at exactly one place in the corpus, app.py:144, on /v1/query only - so both are unbounded key-guessing oracles that return 401 on a miss and a fresh credential on a hit. rotate_key compounds this: on a successful guess it first REVOKES the presented key (app.py:232-236) and then issues a replacement (app.py:237-241), so a hit also locks out the legitimate holder. The two statements share one implicit transaction scope with no explicit BEGIN, so a failure between them revokes the key with no replacement. rotate_key also reads `body["api_key"]` at app.py:235 where line 226 used `.get`, raising KeyError and a 500 when the field is absent.
findings.impact: An attacker brute-forces API keys at line rate against two unrated endpoints, and a single successful guess both grants a new long-lived key and revokes the victim's.
findings.recommendation: Require the key in the Authorization header via _require_principal, apply limits.allow keyed on the client and the presented key prefix, and make rotation issue the replacement before revoking the old key inside one explicit transaction.

triage.reason: Ingress at app.py:208 and app.py:226 - the api_key body field on unauthenticated routes.

This is not a generic 'no rate limit' DoS complaint: the module implements a limiter (limits.py:19-32) and applies it to a sibling route, so the omission on the credential endpoints is a bypass of an existing control.
Self-service revocation of another party's credential on a guessed value is an access-control defect, not missing hygiene.
app.py:140-146,204-242 and limits.py:19-32 read directly; the single limiter call site confirmed by grep.

scope.narrowed_by: Keys are stored hashed (`digest(%s,'sha256')`, app.py:62) and generated with secrets.token_urlsafe(32) (app.py:212,230), so the search space itself is large.

findings.title: A hardcoded playground key maps to a real principal that can write into the shared corpus
findings.evidence: settings.py:47 defines `demo_api_key: str = "demo-playground-key"` and app.py:55-57 short-circuits authentication on it before any database lookup: `if api_key == settings.demo_api_key: return Principal(settings.demo_tenant, "playground", frozenset({"public"}))`. Because it is a constant rather than a database row, it cannot be revoked or rotated through /v1/keys/rotate - that path updates rag.api_keys (app.py:233), which never contained it. The read side is properly confined: collections_for (retriever.py:37-42) restricts the demo tenant to the public FAQ collection. The write side is not - the demo principal satisfies `_require_principal` on /v1/documents (app.py:175) and on /v1/manifest (app.py:198), and the latter takes its tenant from the body.
findings.impact: A credential printed in the public documentation is a valid writer against the ingestion endpoints, which is what makes the manifest and prompt-injection findings reachable by an unauthenticated internet user rather than by a paying tenant.
findings.recommendation: Give the playground a real, revocable database-backed key with an explicitly read-only capability, and reject it on every ingestion route.

triage.reason: Rule 08 declares a hardcoded static secret VALID on its own terms; here it is additionally live on the authentication path.
Not a mock database or a local-only test fixture: it is checked in the production authentication function ahead of the real lookup.
collections_for (retriever.py:39-41) is a genuine mitigation and is credited in the narrowing - it confines the demo principal's READS. Nothing confines its writes.
settings.py:46-49, app.py:55-57,71-78,173-201 and retriever.py:37-42 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Reads are confined to the public-faq collection by retriever.py:39-41, and the ACL intersection at retriever.py:34 still applies to what it retrieves.

findings.title: An arbitrary-SQL tool sits in the tool module one registry entry from being model-callable
findings.evidence: tools.py:53-61 executes `conn.execute(query)` on a raw string parameter with no parameterisation, no statement allow-list and no read-only enforcement, and returns up to 4000 characters of the result. Its own docstring (tools.py:54-58) records that it was written for an analytics spike and that 'It never made it into the tool list because the model kept preferring it over lookup_work_order' - so exclusion was a quality decision, not a security one. I traced reachability rather than assuming it: run_sql is absent from TOOL_SPECS (tools.py:64-89) and from TOOL_REGISTRY (tools.py:91-94), and dispatch resolves only through the registry (tools.py:99-101), returning an unknown-tool error otherwise. It is therefore not callable today.
findings.impact: Adding this function to TOOL_REGISTRY - a one-line change the docstring invites - would let injected document text execute arbitrary SQL against the warehouse snapshot schema with the service's own database credentials.
findings.recommendation: Delete the function; if ad-hoc analytics is needed, expose a parameterised query with a fixed statement set against a read-only role.

triage.reason: Rule 08 makes a direct injection path in a module's own logic VALID even with no live caller, which is why this is reported; the absent registry entry is why it is `probable` and medium rather than high.
Reachability was traced through TOOL_SPECS, TOOL_REGISTRY and dispatch rather than inferred, and the negative result is recorded in the narrowing.
Rule 08 exempts intrinsic flaws from the trust-boundary tracing requirement.
tools.py:53-109 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Not reachable via dispatch: run_sql appears in neither TOOL_SPECS nor TOOL_REGISTRY, so tools.py:99 returns an unknown-tool error for it.

findings.title: Tool arguments from the model are splatted as keyword arguments with the declared schema never enforced
findings.evidence: tools.py:104 parses the model's argument string with json.loads and tools.py:109 calls `await fn(principal, **arguments)`. The JSON-Schema blocks declared in TOOL_SPECS (tools.py:70-74 and :82-87) are advertised to the model but never validated server-side - there is no jsonschema validate call in this module, unlike app.py:149 and app.py:179 which do validate request bodies. Any key the model emits becomes a Python keyword argument, so an unexpected key raises TypeError inside the request handler, and a missing required key does the same.
findings.impact: Model-chosen argument names propagate directly into the Python call, producing unhandled 500s and removing the last server-side check on what a prompt-injected tool call may pass to a tool.
findings.recommendation: Validate `arguments` against the tool's own declared JSON Schema before dispatch and reject anything that does not conform, rather than relying on the model to honour the spec.

triage.reason: Ingress at app.py:118 - `call.function.arguments`, whose content is steerable by injected document text through the model.
json.loads is used safely and is not the complaint; the finding is that a declared schema exists and is never applied, which is the reverse of pedantry about a safe library.
Not a resource-exhaustion claim - the effect is an unvalidated call signature, not an unbounded input.
tools.py:97-109 and app.py:117-121 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Only two tools are registered and both take a single string parameter, so the present blast radius is a 500 rather than unintended behaviour.

findings.title: Deep-link router loads an unvalidated target URL into the WebView that holds the session-token bridge
findings.evidence: DeepLinkRouter.kt:62 is `val target = uri.getQueryParameter("target") ?: "${BuildConfig.API_BASE}${uri.path}"` and line 63 passes it straight to ReportWebViewActivity.intentFor, which stores it as EXTRA_URL (ReportWebViewActivity.kt:26-27) and loads it at ReportWebViewActivity.kt:61. There is no scheme check, no host check and no allow-list on `target`. The doc comment at DeepLinkRouter.kt:56-60 asserts the opposite - that App Links verification makes anything on the https scheme 'one of our own report links' - and that premise fails twice: the https intent-filter carries no android:host (AndroidManifest.xml:47-52), and App Links verification would in any case never constrain a query parameter. The activity is exported (AndroidManifest.xml:33) and also accepts a bare `atlas` scheme with no host restriction at the filter level (AndroidManifest.xml:39-44).
findings.impact: A tapped link or scanned QR code on any domain renders attacker HTML inside the activity that has the Atlas JavaScript bridge bound, which is the first half of a full session-token theft.
findings.recommendation: Parse `target` with Uri.parse and discard it unless scheme is https and host equals BuildConfig.API_HOST, falling back to the API-anchored path form.

triage.reason: Ingress at DeepLinkRouter.kt:27 (`intent?.data`), deliverable by any third-party app or web page because the activity is exported.
The claimed mitigation is stated in the doc comment and was checked against the manifest; the filter has no host, so it does not hold.
Not hypothetical misuse by a caller - the untrusted caller is the threat model for an exported activity.
DeepLinkRouter.kt:17-103, ReportWebViewActivity.kt:20-69 and AndroidManifest.xml:31-58 read directly by me as well as by the partition researcher; line numbers agree.

scope.narrowed_by: Gated on SessionStore.isSignedIn() at DeepLinkRouter.kt:28 - which is precisely the state in which a token exists to steal.
