findings.title: WebView JavaScript bridge returns the raw session bearer to whatever origin is loaded
findings.evidence: ReportWebViewActivity.kt:44 enables JavaScript and :57 calls `web.addJavascriptInterface(ReportBridge(), "Atlas")` unconditionally - before the URL is even read at :59 - so the bridge is live for every page the activity ever loads and for anything that page navigates or frames to. No WebViewClient is set anywhere in the file, so there is no shouldOverrideUrlLoading allow-list and no origin check at all. ReportBridge exposes exactly two @JavascriptInterface methods and both are session secrets: `sessionToken()` returns `SessionStore.bearer().orEmpty()` (:96) and `actorId()` returns the actor id (:99). minSdk is 26 (build.gradle.kts:12), so only annotated methods are reachable - which does not help, because both annotated methods are the secrets.
findings.impact: One page load from an attacker-chosen URL yields the full account bearer and actor id, i.e. complete session takeover against the backend API.
findings.recommendation: Bind the bridge only after confirming the loaded URL's host equals BuildConfig.API_HOST, install a WebViewClient refusing off-host navigation, and stop returning the raw token - perform the signature fetch natively instead.

triage.reason: Ingress at DeepLinkRouter.kt:62; the attacker-controlled URL becomes EXTRA_URL and reaches loadUrl at ReportWebViewActivity.kt:61.
No mitigation to credit - there is no WebViewClient, no origin check and no conditional binding.
Handing a bearer token to arbitrary JavaScript is not a missing-hardening item.
ReportWebViewActivity.kt:35-100 read directly; both bridge methods verified.

scope.narrowed_by: The activity itself is android:exported="false" (AndroidManifest.xml:57), so a third-party app cannot launch it directly - it is reached through the exported deep-link router.

findings.title: Exported ContentProvider serves any app-private file through path traversal in lastPathSegment
findings.evidence: AndroidManifest.xml:62-66 declares the provider with `android:exported="true"`, no android:permission, no readPermission, no <path-permission> and no <grant-uri-permission> element - so any app may call it directly and no URI grant is required, which makes grantUriPermissions beside the point. AttachmentSync.kt:35-37 takes `uri.lastPathSegment`, joins it with `File(attachmentDir(context!!), name)` and opens it. Uri path segments are split on the ENCODED path and each segment is then percent-decoded, so a single segment written as `%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fshared_prefs%2fatlas.session.xml` returns the decoded string `../../shared_prefs/atlas.session.xml`, which File joins and the kernel resolves out of filesDir/attachments. There is no canonicalisation, no startsWith containment test and no name allow-list. query (AttachmentSync.kt:47) has the same defect for names and sizes.
findings.impact: Any installed app, declaring zero permissions, reads every file under the app's private data directory - databases, caches and the session preferences blob - and enumerates their names and sizes.
findings.recommendation: Resolve with canonicalFile and reject unless canonicalPath starts with attachmentDir(context).canonicalPath, and set android:exported="false" so access is granted only per-URI via FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION.

triage.reason: Ingress at AttachmentSync.kt:35 - the Uri supplied by a third-party app's ContentResolver.openFileDescriptor call.
MODE_READ_ONLY (AttachmentSync.kt:37) and the stubbed insert/update/delete (:53-62) are credited in the narrowing; neither constrains WHICH file is opened.
An exported provider's callers are untrusted by definition.
AttachmentSync.kt:20-63 and AndroidManifest.xml:62-66 read directly; I separately confirmed the class is defined in AttachmentSync.kt rather than a missing file.

scope.narrowed_by: Read-only: openFile passes MODE_READ_ONLY and insert/update/delete are stubs, so this discloses rather than modifies.

findings.title: The staging build ships a trust-all TLS trust manager and hostname verifier
findings.evidence: build.gradle.kts:35-48 creates a `staging` build type with `initWith(getByName("release"))`, `isDebuggable = false` and `matchingFallbacks += listOf("release")` - a distributable artifact, not a developer-only build - and sets `ALLOW_INSECURE_TLS` to true at :47. ApiClient.kt:34-45 branches on that flag: it installs `permissiveTrust` (ApiClient.kt:28-32), whose checkServerTrusted returns Unit for any chain, plus `hostnameVerifier { _, _ -> true }` (:41), and then `return this` at :42 - so `certificatePinner(pinner)` at :44 is never reached. Both HTTP clients are affected (:53 and :63). Installing a custom SSLSocketFactory and X509TrustManager also removes the connection from the platform trust path, so the <pin-set> in network_security_config.xml:14-17 does not apply either - inverting that file's own claim at lines 10-11 that the two layers back each other up.
findings.impact: Any attacker on the same network as a field tester reads and rewrites all API traffic for the staging build: harvesting the bearer, injecting report HTML into the token-bearing WebView, and choosing the upload URL the bearer is then sent to.
findings.recommendation: Delete permissiveTrust and the hostnameVerifier override, and trust the internal CA through a <trust-anchors> entry scoped to api.staging.fieldops.example in the network security config instead.

triage.reason: A trust-all X509TrustManager is the intrinsically-broken-primitive case; it is additionally live in a shipped build type.
Not dismissed as a debug-only path: isDebuggable=false and initWith(release) at build.gradle.kts:36,39 establish that this is a distributed artifact.
Both candidate mitigations were traced and neither applies - the early return skips the pinner, and the custom socket factory bypasses NSC pinning.
build.gradle.kts:25,28-54, ApiClient.kt:21-66 and network_security_config.xml read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: The release build type keeps ALLOW_INSECURE_TLS false (build.gradle.kts:25), so production builds do reach certificatePinner at ApiClient.kt:44.

findings.title: Feature gates fail open, so an unprovisioned device passes the crew-administration check
findings.evidence: FeatureGates.kt:29 is `fun isEnabled(name: String): Boolean = snapshot[name] ?: true`, and `snapshot` (:12) is a plain in-memory map with no persistence, cleared outright by clear() (:22) and repopulated by update() only with the keys the payload actually carries (:16-19). So after every process death, after a sign-out, and whenever the server simply omits a flag, isEnabled returns true. canManageCrews() (:32) and canReopenClosed() (:35) both route through it, while demoMode() (:38) deliberately defaults to false - which establishes that failing closed was available and was chosen for the non-privileged flag only. DeepLinkRouter.openCrewAdmin (:76-83) uses canManageCrews as its sole gate before starting CrewAdminActivity, and the router is exported and accepts `atlas://crew` (AndroidManifest.xml:33,43).
findings.impact: A co-installed app firing atlas://crew at a cold-started signed-in device opens the crew administration surface on a plain technician's phone, before any refresh has populated the flag map.
findings.recommendation: Default to false (`snapshot[name] ?: false`) and gate the administration surface on SessionStore.role() and a server-side check rather than on a client-held feature flag.

triage.reason: Ingress at DeepLinkRouter.kt:27 - an atlas://crew Uri from any third-party app, since the router is exported.
canManageCrews IS the mitigation on this path and it is what fails open; demoMode on line 38 proves the safe idiom was available.
A privilege gate that answers 'allowed' when it has no data is a live authorization defect, not a hardening omission.
FeatureGates.kt:10-39 and DeepLinkRouter.kt:76-83 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Requires a stored token (DeepLinkRouter.kt:28) and closes once a board refresh calls update() with an explicit crew_admin:false. Severity is held at medium rather than high because CrewAdminActivity is NOT present in this corpus, so whether the backend re-checks the role could not be verified.

findings.title: https intent filter declares no android:host, so any domain can deliver a link to the router
findings.evidence: AndroidManifest.xml:47-52 declares `<intent-filter android:autoVerify="true">` whose only data element is `<data android:scheme="https" android:pathPrefix="/r/" />` (:51) - no android:host. Intent-filter data matching treats an absent host as 'any host', so the filter matches https://<anything>/r/<anything>. autoVerify has no host to verify against, so App Links verification cannot succeed and the activity never becomes the auto-opening default; it appears in the disambiguation chooser instead. The filter width is what matters: it is the mechanism that lets an attacker-owned domain hand a Uri to routeWeb, and it is the concrete fact that falsifies the 'verified against our domain association file' reasoning at DeepLinkRouter.kt:57-59.
findings.impact: Any web page or QR code on any domain can hand this app a URI that the router treats as a trusted first-party report link.
findings.recommendation: Add android:host for the real domains to the <data> element so autoVerify has something to verify and the filter stops matching foreign hosts.

triage.reason: This is a manifest configuration finding; the data-flow consequence is tracked on the routeWeb finding.
autoVerify="true" is the apparent mitigation and it is inert without a host, so it does not hold.
An over-broad intent filter on an exported activity is an exposure decision, not a missing hardening attribute.

findings.title: Attachment uploader attaches the bearer to a server-designated URL on any host
findings.evidence: AuthInterceptor states and correctly implements the policy that the bearer goes only to BuildConfig.API_HOST - its doc comment at AuthInterceptor.kt:8-12 says 'Redirects and presigned URLs point at storage hosts we do not control, so the token must not follow them', and AuthInterceptor.kt:19 enforces it with an exact host inequality. AttachmentUploader sidesteps that entirely: it uses ApiClient.uploads (ApiClient.kt:57-65), which carries no AuthInterceptor, and sets the header by hand at AttachmentSync.kt:80 for a `uploadUrl` string with no host check of any kind. Per the class comment at AttachmentSync.kt:66-68 that URL is whatever POST /attachments/intent returns, so control of that response is control of where the bearer is sent.
findings.impact: One attacker-influenced uploadUrl in an API response sends the technician's bearer token and actor id to a host of the attacker's choosing.
findings.recommendation: Use a presigned URL that needs no Authorization header; if a header is unavoidable, assert uploadUrl.toHttpUrl().host against an allow-list of storage hosts before building the request.

triage.reason: Ingress at AttachmentSync.kt:72 - the uploadUrl parameter, sourced from the API response per the class comment.

Certificate pinning on the release channel (ApiClient.kt:23-26,44) is credited and is exactly why this is `probable` rather than `confirmed`; it makes the URL-issuing call hard to tamper with in production but does nothing on the staging build.

AttachmentSync.kt:70-88, ApiClient.kt:47-65 and AuthInterceptor.kt read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: In a release build the API channel is pinned, so this needs a compromised or SSRF-able backend rather than a network position; on the staging build the TLS finding removes even that.

findings.title: Offline report notes are interpolated unescaped and rendered under the API origin

The document is then loaded with `loadDataWithBaseURL("https://api.fieldops.example/", ...)` (:85-86), which stamps injected script with the API's own origin, and the Atlas bridge is already bound from :57. The notes value is the same server-side field that the API renders unescaped through a denylist sanitiser (fieldops-api/src/lib/policy.ts:57-63), so the two defects share one source. Marked probable because reachability is unproven: notes arrive only via EXTRA_OFFLINE_NOTES from offlineIntent (:29-32), and a corpus-wide grep finds no caller of offlineIntent - intentFor always sets EXTRA_URL, which takes the early-return branch at :60-63.

Reachability was traced by grep rather than assumed, and the negative result is recorded in the narrowing and in the `probable` status rather than used to dismiss the finding.

findings.title: The full-rebuild branch of customer_pii_masked emits raw email, phone and bank_account
findings.evidence: The model has two branches. The incremental branch masks - customer_pii_masked.sql:25-27 applies masked_email, masked_phone and masked_account. The full-rebuild `{% else %}` branch (line 35) selects the same three columns RAW: `email,` at :44, `phone,` at :45, `bank_account,` at :46, with no macro applied. Its own comment at :37-39 states when that branch runs: 'on the first build of a new environment and whenever the masking policy version changes' - i.e. every `dbt build --full-refresh` and every rotation of pii_policy_version. The model is described in schema.yml:34 as 'The customer view every downstream consumer is pointed at' and schema.yml:41-43 documents email as 'First character plus domain' and bank_account as 'Last four digits only'. partner_extract.sql:41 selects from this model and ships `c.email as customer_email` (:53) and `c.bank_account as destination_account` (:54) into the exports schema, which dbt_project.yml:49-50 grants to partner_readers.
findings.impact: After any full refresh, the table every consumer treats as masked contains cleartext customer email addresses, phone numbers and bank account numbers, and the partner extract built from it hands those to an external partner.
findings.recommendation: Apply the three masking macros in the full-rebuild branch as well - the two branches must differ only in their incremental predicate - and add a dbt test asserting that email does not match a plain address pattern.

triage.reason: No attacker-controlled input is involved; the exposure is of data the model itself emits, so the trust-boundary rule does not apply.
The masking macros are the mitigation and were verified to work (mask_pii.sql:7-28); the finding is that one of the two code paths does not call them.
Cleartext PII crossing into a partner-readable schema is a disclosure, not a hardening omission.
customer_pii_masked.sql:19-53, mask_pii.sql, partner_extract.sql:34-58 and schema.yml:33-46 read directly; the macro-usage grep confirms masked_* appears only in the incremental branch.

scope.narrowed_by: Only the full-rebuild path is affected; a steady-state incremental run does mask correctly, so the window opens on first build and on every --full-refresh.

findings.title: apply_grants falls back to granting SELECT to public on any unrecognised target
findings.evidence: apply_grants.sql:11-15 maps three target names to reader roles and apply_grants.sql:17 resolves the reader as `reader_by_target.get(target.name, "public")`. Any target name outside {prod, ci, dev} - a new environment, a developer's personal target, a renamed profile - therefore resolves to the PostgreSQL `public` pseudo-role, and lines 20-21 then execute `grant usage on schema ... to public` and `grant select on ... to public`. The macro is wired as a post-hook on every folder in the project (dbt_project.yml:33, :41, :48), so it runs on the PII marts and on the partner exports alike. Nothing validates target.name and there is no else-branch or compiler error.
findings.impact: One unrecognised target name grants every database role SELECT on every model in the project, including dim_customer, which carries raw email, phone and bank_account.
findings.recommendation: Raise a compiler error when target.name is not in the map rather than defaulting, and never let `public` be a reader value.

triage.reason: Configuration-state finding; no attacker-controlled data flow is claimed.
The per-target mapping is the intended control and was evaluated; the default parameter is what defeats it.
Granting the public role read on PII tables is an access-control decision that takes effect, not an absent nicety.
apply_grants.sql:9-34 and dbt_project.yml:20-51 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Requires a target name outside the three mapped values; profiles.yml:5 defaults to `dev`, which is mapped.

findings.title: The exports folder is the only one without row-level security, and partner_extract is not tenant-filtered
findings.evidence: dbt_project.yml wires `+pre-hook: "{{ enable_row_security(this) }}"` on staging (:32) and on marts (:40) but NOT on exports (:45-50), which carries only the apply_grants post-hook at :48. partner_extract.sql filters solely on partner - `where p.partner_id = '{{ partner }}'` at :30 - with no tenant predicate anywhere, and it deliberately emits `e.tenant_id` as an output column at :47 alongside customer_name, customer_email and destination_account (:52-54). The folder is granted to `partner_readers` (dbt_project.yml:50). The macro tenant_predicate() exists at row_security.sql:34-36 and a corpus-wide grep shows it is never used in any model.

findings.recommendation: Add the row-security pre-hook to the exports folder and filter partner_extract on the tenant scope as well as the partner, or drop tenant_id and the customer columns from the partner-facing model.

triage.reason: The consumer is an authorised partner role; the finding is the absence of a scoping control, not a taint path.
Both candidate controls were checked: RLS is absent from this folder, and tenant_predicate() exists but has zero call sites.
The exports folder is production output, and its grant to partner_readers was traced rather than assumed.
dbt_project.yml:20-51, partner_extract.sql:1-58 and row_security.sql:34-36 read directly; macro-usage grep run over the partition.

scope.narrowed_by: Bounded by `limit {{ var("max_rows", 5000) | int }}` at partner_extract.sql:58, which caps rows per build but not which tenants they belong to.

findings.title: Row-level security is enabled by a pre-hook that a table rebuild discards, and is never FORCEd
findings.evidence: Three defects in one macro. (1) Ordering: it is wired as a `+pre-hook` on marts, which are `+materialized: table` (dbt_project.yml:39-40). dbt's table materialization builds into an intermediate relation, renames the existing relation to a backup and renames the intermediate onto the target name; a pre-hook runs before all of that, so `{{ this }}` resolves to the PREVIOUS run's table - the one about to be dropped. The freshly created table has RLS disabled and no policies, so marts are unprotected after every run. The same project proves the distinction: apply_grants is wired as a post-hook (dbt_project.yml:41) and does survive the rename. (2) `alter table {{ relation }} enable row level security` at row_security.sql:18 omits FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, so the table owner - the dbt role from profiles.yml:12 - bypasses the policy entirely. (3) The policy is created `for select` only (row_security.sql:23), while apply_grants.sql:25-26 grants insert and update on every relation to settlement_app and warehouse_loader, so writes are not covered by any policy.
findings.impact: The marts holding raw customer contact details carry no row-level policy after any run, the owning role bypasses the policy where it does exist, and write paths are ungoverned.
findings.recommendation: Move the hook to a post-hook ordered after apply_grants, add `force row level security`, and extend the policy to all commands rather than select alone.

triage.reason: Configuration and ordering finding rather than a taint path.
The macro's fail-closed NULL behaviour was verified and credited (see ruled_out); these three defects are separate from and survive that check.
Deterministic - the policy loss happens on every table rebuild, not probabilistically.

row_security.sql:9-36, dbt_project.yml:29-50 and apply_grants.sql:25-26 read directly. Point (1) rests on dbt's documented table-materialization ordering, independently confirmed by the critic stage at high confidence.

scope.narrowed_by: Staging is `+materialized: incremental` (dbt_project.yml:31), which inserts into the existing relation, so the policy does persist there on normal runs - but is destroyed by any --full-refresh, which takes the same rename path.

findings.title: apply_grants gives settlement_app and warehouse_loader write access to every relation in the project
findings.evidence: apply_grants.sql:25-26 unconditionally executes `grant insert, update on {{ relation }} to settlement_app` and the same for warehouse_loader, for whatever relation the macro is called on. Because the macro is a post-hook on staging, marts and exports (dbt_project.yml:33,41,48), those two service roles receive write access to every model in the project - including dim_customer, which holds raw email, phone and bank_account, and including partner_extract. The comment at apply_grants.sql:23-24 justifies it as 'the loader and the settlement service write into these relations between dbt runs', which explains staging but not the marts or the partner exports. This composes with the settlement-worker task role holding Action:* Resource:* in pulumi-platform/iam.ts:80.
findings.impact: A compromise of either service role rewrites analytics marts and the partner-facing extract, and the settlement service - whose AWS role is already account-admin - can alter the customer dimension.
findings.recommendation: Scope the write grants to the staging schema the loader actually writes, and drop them from marts and exports.

triage.reason: Permission-model finding; no untrusted input path is claimed.
The per-folder +grants blocks in dbt_project.yml are the apparent scoping control and were checked; the macro's hardcoded grants are additive and ignore them.
Write grants that take effect on every rebuild are an active permission decision.
apply_grants.sql:19-32 and dbt_project.yml:20-51 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: DELETE and TRUNCATE are revoked from settlement_app by the worker's own bootstrap SQL (settlement-worker/settlement/ledger.py:21-22), though only for the settlement schema.

findings.title: Staging carries raw bank account numbers, emails and phones into a broadly granted schema
findings.evidence: stg_payout_events.sql:66-69 selects `a.bank_account_number`, `c.display_name as customer_name`, `c.email as customer_email` and `c.phone as customer_phone` directly from the settlement and CRM sources (:40, :51) with no masking macro applied anywhere in the file - a corpus-wide macro-usage grep confirms masked_email, masked_phone, masked_account and pseudonym appear only in customer_pii_masked.sql. The masking macros exist and work; the finding is that this model does not call them, verified by grep.
Cleartext bank account numbers readable by a broad analyst role is a disclosure, not a hardening gap.
stg_payout_events.sql:1-72, dbt_project.yml:29-35 and schema.yml:10-16 read directly.

findings.title: The customer pseudonym is an unsalted SHA-256 keyed on a public project variable
findings.evidence: mask_pii.sql:32-33 computes `encode(digest({{ column_name }} || '{{ var("pii_policy_version") }}', 'sha256'), 'hex')`. The only entropy added to the hashed value is pii_policy_version, whose value is committed in plain text at dbt_project.yml:18 (`pii_policy_version: v3`) - so it is a public constant, not a secret salt. The macro is applied to customer_id (customer_pii_masked.sql:28 and :47) and the resulting column is documented at schema.yml:44-45 as 'Stable hash, safe to join on across environments'. Customer identifiers are a small, enumerable domain, so anyone holding the pseudonym column and the version string can recover the original identifier by exhaustive hashing.
findings.impact: The pseudonymised identifier is reversible by anyone who can read the column, defeating the de-identification the masked mart is built to provide and re-linking masked rows to the raw dimension.
findings.recommendation: Key the digest with a secret held outside the repository - an HMAC with a warehouse-side key, or pgcrypto with a secret salt - and stop documenting the output as safe to share.

triage.reason: Rule 08 names a fundamentally inadequate primitive as VALID; an unsalted digest over an enumerable domain is that case.
SHA-256 is a safe hash used unsafely - the defect is the absent secret salt over a small input space, not a demand for extra paranoia.
Rule 08 exempts intrinsic flaws from trust-boundary tracing.
mask_pii.sql:31-34, dbt_project.yml:14-18, customer_pii_masked.sql:28,47 and schema.yml:44-46 read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Requires read access to the pseudonym column; the value is at least stable and distinct per policy version, so rotation invalidates precomputed tables.

findings.title: partner_extract silently rewrites the partner identifier instead of rejecting it
findings.evidence: partner_extract.sql:16 normalises the run's partner variable with `modules.re.sub("[^a-z0-9-]", "", requested_partner | lower)` and line 30 filters `where p.partner_id = '{{ partner }}'`. The substitution is an allow-list that cannot be escaped - injection is ruled out separately - but it SILENTLY REWRITES rather than rejecting. `ACME_Analytics` becomes `acmeanalytics`, and `a-b_c` and `a-bc` both collapse to `a-bc`, so two distinct partner identifiers can normalise onto the same value. The model is a table materialised into the partner-readable exports schema and carries customer_email and destination_account (:53-54).
findings.impact: A typo or an underscore in the partner_id variable builds one partner's extract - complete with another partner's customers, emails and destination bank accounts - into the table that partner reads.
findings.recommendation: Raise a compiler error when the sanitised value differs from the input, rather than substituting, so a malformed partner identifier fails the build instead of silently retargeting it.

triage.reason: Ingress at partner_extract.sql:15 - the partner_id dbt var, supplied on the command line per the model's own comment at :10-11.
The sanitiser is credited as fully effective against injection (recorded in ruled_out); this finding is about its fail-open normalisation, which is a different property.
Not a stretched adjacent class - the effect reported is the direct consequence of substitution rather than rejection, in the same statement.
partner_extract.sql:1-58 read directly; the normalisation semantics were confirmed by the critic stage.

scope.narrowed_by: The operator running dbt is trusted, so this is a fat-finger and collision risk rather than an external attack path.

findings.title: CHAIN: published playground key to cross-tenant corpus poisoning to server-side request forgery
findings.evidence: Three individually-reported defects compose into one unauthenticated path. Step 1: `demo-playground-key` is a hardcoded constant that authenticates to a real Principal without a database lookup (settings.py:47, app.py:56-57), so the attacker needs no account. Step 2: POST /v1/manifest accepts that principal, discards it (app.py:198) and writes chunks under a body-supplied tenant_id with a default ACL of `["*"]` (ingest.py:98,100) - a wildcard that DOCUMENT_SCHEMA explicitly forbids on the other ingestion route (app.py:41) and that `_acl_allows` treats as matching everyone (retriever.py:32). Step 3: when the victim tenant next queries, that chunk is retrieved and interpolated into the system message (prompt.py:25,38), where the standing instruction at prompt.py:16-17 tells the model to call http_get on links in the context; http_get fetches any URL with no allow-list (tools.py:24) and the body is returned into the model's context at app.py:119-121. Each step is verified against the source; the chain is statically confirmed rather than executed, since stage 9 could not run offline.
findings.impact: An anonymous internet user, using only a credential printed in the documentation, plants instructions in another tenant's retrieval corpus and causes the service to fetch attacker-chosen internal URLs and surface the responses - a full unauthenticated read pivot into the internal network.
findings.recommendation: Fix the weakest link first: bind /v1/manifest to the authenticated principal's tenant and reject wildcard ACLs there as DOCUMENT_SCHEMA already does. Then constrain http_get to an allow-list, and make the demo key read-only.

triage.reason: Full ingress-to-sink trace given with file:line at every hop, beginning at an unauthenticated HTTP request.
Every step is deterministic; none depends on timing or on unrealistic environmental conditions.
No mitigation is being stretched around - each constituent defect is independently confirmed, and the chain only composes them.
Every cited line was read directly during the review.

scope.narrowed_by: Constituent findings are individually confirmed; the end-to-end chain is statically confirmed only - mantis-chain does not author end-to-end reproducers and stage 9 was unavailable offline.

findings.title: CHAIN: production PII reaches an anonymously readable S3 bucket through the staging warehouse
findings.evidence: The data layer and the infrastructure layer fail in the same direction. On the warehouse side, a full rebuild of customer_pii_masked emits raw email, phone and bank_account (customer_pii_masked.sql:44-46) and partner_extract carries those columns into the exports schema (partner_extract.sql:53-54), which has no row-level security (dbt_project.yml:45-50) and no tenant filter (partner_extract.sql:30), so it spans tenants. On the infrastructure side, the staging stack sets publicExports true (Pulumi.staging.yaml:9), which inverts all four PublicAccessBlock guards (storage.ts:44-47) and attaches `Principal: '*'` s3:GetObject (storage.ts:60-62), and sets replicateProdExports true (Pulumi.staging.yaml:12), which accepts inbound replication of production objects (storage.ts:82). The exports bucket is tagged `Contains: 'work-order-and-billing-exports'` (storage.ts:29). Both halves are confirmed by direct reading; what is NOT established in this corpus is the pipeline step that writes a dbt exports table into the S3 exports bucket - no such job exists in the target - so the join between the two halves is inferred from the warehouse-loader IAM policy (iam.ts:35-41, index.ts:72-84) and the shared naming, not from code.
findings.impact: Unmasked production customer contact details and destination bank accounts become anonymously downloadable objects, with no credential and no log of who took them.
findings.recommendation: Break the chain at the cheapest point: set publicExports false for staging and stop replicating production objects into a stack that can be made public; then fix the masking branch so the exported data is not raw in the first place.

triage.reason: The terminal consumer is an anonymous internet caller; the origin of the data is traced to the production replication source at storage.ts:82.
The staging stack was not dismissed as non-production - replicateProdExports is exactly what makes its contents production data.
Both halves are independently confirmed findings; the honest gap in the join is stated rather than papered over, which is why the missing link is named in the evidence and the narrowing.
All cited lines read directly; the absence of an S3-writing job in the corpus was verified rather than assumed.

scope.narrowed_by: The link between the dbt exports schema and the S3 exports bucket is not present in this corpus - no loader job is included - so that hop is inferred from the warehouse-loader IAM grant and bucket naming rather than read from code.

findings.title: CHAIN: work-order note to script execution in the mobile WebView to session-token theft
findings.evidence: The server's sanitiser and the client's renderer both fail on the same field. scrubNotes (policy.ts:57-63) is a three-pattern denylist that removes <script> blocks, <iframe> tags and the literal `javascript:` but no event-handler attribute; workorders.ts:197 then interpolates the stored note into the printable sheet unescaped while every neighbouring field is escaped (:189,:192,:194,:195). On the device, DeepLinkRouter.openOrder (DeepLinkRouter.kt:72-73) builds exactly that print URL and hands it to ReportWebViewActivity, which has JavaScript enabled (ReportWebViewActivity.kt:44) and the Atlas bridge bound (:57) whose sessionToken() returns the raw bearer (:96). So a note written by any authenticated actor executes in the technician's WebView with access to the token. The org check at workorders.ts:175 confines the victim to the author's own organisation.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user in an organisation - including a technician, who can write notes on any order in the org through the unguarded PATCH route - harvests the session bearer of every colleague who opens that work order on the mobile app.
findings.recommendation: Escape notes at the point of interpolation in the print route, and stop exposing the bearer through the JavaScript bridge; either fix alone breaks the chain.

triage.reason: Ingress at workorders.ts:101 and :139 (the notes body field); the sink is ReportWebViewActivity.kt:96, reached through the print URL built at DeepLinkRouter.kt:72.
The sanitiser is a hand-rolled denylist, not a standard safe library.
Deterministic: the payload is stored and fires whenever the sheet is opened.
All cited lines in both partitions read directly.

scope.narrowed_by: Confined to a single organisation by the org predicate at workorders.ts:175, and the victim must open the order's report in the mobile app.
